abort.no_meter_found: No meter answered at any Modbus address or baud rate on that port. Check the wiring, and that the meter is powered.

error.no_serial_number: The meter did not report a serial number, which is needed to identify it.
error.unsupported_meter: A device answers there, but its model code {code} is not one of the supported meters: the EM530, EM540, EM330, EM340, ET330 and ET340.

progress.search: Searching Modbus addresses 1 to 247 at each baud rate the meters offer. This takes up to about 6 minutes, and stops at the first meter that answers.

data_description.host: The hostname or IP address of the RS485-to-TCP gateway.
data_description.port: The port the gateway listens on.

gateway.description: Set up a Carlo Gavazzi energy meter, such as an EM540 or ET340, behind an RS485-to-TCP gateway in transparent (RTU) mode. Set the gateway's serial side to the meter's baud rate.

reconfigure.description: Update how this meter is reached. Change the baud rate here after changing it on the meter.

data_description.device: The serial port the meter's RS485 bus is wired to. ESPHome serial proxies are listed here too.

serial.description: Set up a Carlo Gavazzi energy meter, such as an EM540 or ET340, wired to a serial port or an ESPHome serial proxy. Home Assistant then looks for the baud rate the meter is set to.

data_description.unit_id: The Modbus address set on the meter, under rS485. The factory default is 1.

data_description.baudrate: The baud rate set on the meter, under rS485. The factory default is 9600. Type another rate if your bus runs at one the meters do not list.

serial_baudrate.description:
The meter at Modbus address {unit_id} answered at **{baudrate} baud**, so that rate is filled in below.

A meter keeps its baud rate in its own settings, and those can only be read once Home Assistant talks to it at that rate. So it tried each rate the meters offer (9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 and 115200) until the meter answered. Change it only if you know the meter is set to another rate.
serial_baudrate.title: Baud rate found

serial_baudrate_unknown.description: Pick the baud rate set on the meter, which it shows in its setup menu under rS485. The factory default of {baudrate} baud is filled in.
serial_baudrate_unknown.title: Baud rate

serial_not_found.description:
No meter answered at Modbus address {unit_id} at any of the baud rates the meters offer (9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 and 115200).

A meter keeps its baud rate in its own settings, and those can only be read once Home Assistant talks to it at that rate, so it tried each one. Check the wiring first: swapping A and B is worth a try.

If the meter's Modbus address was changed, Home Assistant can search every address at every rate, which takes up to about 6 minutes. Or enter the baud rate the meter shows in its setup menu yourself.
serial_not_found.title: Baud rate not found

menu_options.serial: Serial port or ESPHome serial proxy

user.title: How is the meter's RS485 bus reached?

command_failed.message: The meter did not carry out the command: {error}

communication_error.message: Could not communicate with the meter: {error}

link_settings_in_use.message: The serial port is already in use at other settings: {error}

wrong_meter.message: A different meter answers at this address than the one this entry was set up for. Reconfigure the entry to point at the right meter.

wrong_meter.description:
After the link to {title} came back, Home Assistant read the serial number of the meter at its address, and it is not the meter this entry was set up for. Its entities stay unavailable, so the other meter's readings do not end up in this meter's history.

If the meter was replaced, remove this entry and set up the new meter. If two meters share the address, give each its own address on the meter, then select **Reconfigure** on this entry. This message goes away once the right meter answers again.
wrong_meter.title: {title}: a different meter answers
